caption: What if it rained nonstop for a year? That earthy smell after the first drops has a name: petrichor, coined by two Australian scientists in 1964. Much of it comes from geosmin, made by soil bacteria, and some people can smell it at just 5 parts per trillion. Raindrops aren't teardrops either: small ones are round, bigger ones flatten into a hamburger-bun shape, and past about 9 mm across they puff into a parachute and break apart. Now imagine a gentle 2.5 mm drizzle every hour, nonstop. That's 60 mm a day, or about 22 metres in a year if none drained away. Plot twist: all the water in the sky at any moment would cover Earth only about 2.5 cm deep, so at that rate the sky would run dry in about 10 hours. Keeping it going everywhere would need roughly 70 times more water than the ~450 cubic km Earth evaporates each day. Could YOU handle a year of rain? 👇
